Stable controller identities and compact movie columns

Source: R/controller_layout.R
button_layout.Rd

Without a movie, returns the fixed gamepad and peripheral registry. With a movie, returns only its controller's columns, in matrix order. column is a local matrix index; id and key identify the same control across recordings. Unpressed controls supported by the controller are retained. Matrices omit registry entries outside that controller's layout. The registry contains 53 consecutive IDs. Keypad digits and equally numbered Power Pad sensors share numbered_0 through numbered_12 (IDs 40-52), with kind numbered. Microphone is ID 53. Serial positions in a BK2 LogKey are decoded independently of those sensor numbers.

Usage

button_layout(movie = NULL)

Arguments

movie

An imported recording, or NULL for the fixed registry.

Value

Data frame with column, id, key, mnemonic, name and kind.

Details

Additional named controls, such as keyboard keys, have character IDs of the form control:<key>. These are stable within their source key namespace. They appear in the movie's layout without expanding unrelated controllers.

Registered controls use fixed numeric IDs; a mixed layout represents all IDs as character strings. Use keys or IDs for matching, rather than coercing the complete ID column to integers. Source keyboard code sets remain distinct.

Which controls share an ID

The same rules apply in every reader, so a console has the same IDs whichever emulator recorded it. name shows the label on the device; key and id are the shared identity. A column that holds several controls of a recording shows their labels joined by a slash, and no two columns of a layout share a name.

  • By label. A button that carries one of the registry's letters or words (A, B, C, X, Y, Z, L, R, Start, Select, Mode) has that ID. The ID follows the letter, not the place on the pad: A is the right-hand button of a Nintendo pad, the left one of a Genesis pad, and the lower one of an Xbox-style pad, which is what a libTAS recording of an SDL game controller holds.

  • By place, for PlayStation pads. Their buttons carry shapes. They have the IDs of the SNES buttons in the same places: Cross is B, Circle is A, Triangle is X and Square is Y.

  • In order, for numbered buttons. The first is A, then B, X, Y, L1, R1, L2 and R2. This covers arcade and joystick buttons, Master System 1 and 2, and PC Engine I to VI. The Neo Geo's row of A, B, C and D is read the same way, so its C and D are X and Y. A device's only fire button or trigger is A.

  • By role, for the rest. The button that starts or pauses play is Start (PC Engine Run, the Lynx's Pause, the Neo Geo Pocket's Option, keypad Enter, Wii Plus); keypad Clear, Wii Minus, the Lynx's Option 1 and an arcade View Change are Select; Wii Home, libTAS Guide, the Lynx's Option 2 and the PC Engine's switch between two and six buttons are Mode (19); Wii 1 and 2 are X and Y. Mouse left, right and middle are A, B and X, and buttons 4 and 5 are L1 and R1. A light-gun trigger is A; GunCon side A, side B and offscreen shot are B, X and Y.

Arcade buttons that BizHawk shows under the name a cabinet gives them follow one table for the whole platform: Attack and Punch are A, Jump and Missile are B, Kick is X.

Of two direction pads, the left one is the direction pad (IDs 1-4) and the right one has the IDs of the N64's C-buttons (20-23): the Virtual Boy's pads and the WonderSwan's X and Y crosses. An arcade cabinet's two joysticks have the direction IDs of the left and the right analogue stick (N, E, S and W of 24-31 and of 32-39). Controls without a counterpart keep IDs of their own; these are keyboard keys, in the code set of their source. The Intellivision disc has the direction IDs of the left stick: one for each of its eight main directions, and the two neighbours together for a direction between them, such as N and NE for NNE. A disc that a core logs as two axes has the directions the console reads from them. Keypad Star and Pound are Select and Start, like Clear and Enter in the same places. On the Channel F stick, forward and back are Up and Down, the twist is L1 and R1, pushing down is A and pulling up is B. A mouse wheel turned up or down is C-Up or C-Down. A touch on a screen or pad is L3, the press of a pointing input. Each device of an openMSX recording is a controller of its own, with the IDs of its kind. Buttons on the console itself, such as Reset, the Master System's Pause or the lid of a DS, are not part of a pad; they are returned by system_channels().

A shared ID says that two buttons are the same control, not that they do the same thing: what a button does depends on the game. Some recordings store what the game was asked to do, not which button was pressed: a Doom demo holds attack, use and jump, whatever keys or buttons the player had bound to them. These game actions are kept apart from device buttons. They have kind action and IDs of the form action:<name>, shared by every game that records the same action.

Several source controls under one ID

When the rules place several source controls of one recording under one ID, source_inputs retains the decoded input array and source_layout identifies its columns and their universal_key mapping. That column is active whenever any of them is pressed. Reading with aliases = FALSE keeps every control of the recording in a column of its own instead: a control that would be placed under another control's ID keeps the key of its source and an ID of the form control:<key>.

Examples

path <- system.file("extdata", "sample.m64", package = "replayr")
button_layout(read_movie(path))
#>    column id        key mnemonic    name   kind
#> 1       1  1 dpad_right        R   Right button
#> 2       2  2  dpad_left        L    Left button
#> 3       3  3  dpad_down        D    Down button
#> 4       4  4    dpad_up        U      Up button
#> 5       5  5      start        T   Start button
#> 6       6  7          b        B       B button
#> 7       7  8          a        A       A button
#> 8       8 11         l1        p      L1 button
#> 9       9 12         r1        q      R1 button
#> 10     10 18          z        Z       Z button
#> 11     11 20    c_right        > C-Right button
#> 12     12 21     c_left        <  C-Left button
#> 13     13 22     c_down        v  C-Down button
#> 14     14 23       c_up        ^    C-Up button
